title: Han China and the Silk Road

cards.h: A man went to find allies and came back 13 years later
cards.b:
In about 138 BCE, the Han emperor Wu sent an officer named Zhang Qian west to find allies against the Xiongnu, the horse-riding nomads who kept raiding China.

The Xiongnu captured him. He escaped after about ten years, kept going, and came home after thirteen. He had opened up the world.

In 221 BCE Qin Shi Huang united China and was buried with a clay army. His dynasty fell fast. In 202 BCE, Liu Bang, a commoner, founded the Han dynasty, which ruled until 220 CE.

Han rulers used Confucian ideas for their officials. Emperor Wu (141-87 BCE) expanded the empire a lot.

Zhang Qian reported on cities, horses and peoples in Central Asia, such as Ferghana's famous horses and a land called Daxia (Bactria). The Han then pushed into the Tarim basin.

Trade followed. Chinese silk, so light and so valuable, travelled west. Horses, grapes and glass came east.
There was no single 'Silk Road'. The name was coined by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877. Few travellers went the whole way. Goods passed through many hands and prices soared.

Han China made big advances: paper (a court official, Cai Lun, presented an improved paper in 105 CE), the seismoscope of Zhang Heng, and a census in 2 CE counting about 58 million people.

Along with silk, the road carried religions and diseases. Large epidemics are recorded in both empires in the 2nd century CE.

In 97 CE a Han envoy, Gan Ying, got as far as the Persian Gulf but turned back, scared by stories of a long sea voyage. Chinese records mention a 'Daqin' (Rome) embassy in 166 CE, probably merchants.

The two empires knew about each other but never really met.

cards.h: Was the Silk Road mainly about silk?
cards.b:
Myth: it carried mostly silk from China to Rome.Fact: it carried everything: spices, horses, glass, gold, ideas and religions. Buddhism, Manichaeism and later Islam travelled. Also, sea routes were big too, especially to India and Rome.

Finally, Rome's elite loved silk so much that some senators objected. That is true.

Five things to remember

  1. Han (202 BCE-220 CE) followed the short-lived Qin.
  2. Zhang Qian's journey opened Central Asia to China.
  3. The Silk Road was a web, not one road.
  4. Paper, census and science marked the Han.
  5. Kushans linked India to the Silk Road.

Think about it

  • Why would empires fight to control trade routes?
  • What travels faster along trade routes, goods or ideas?

quiz.w: Presented to the court in 105 CE.
Traditional date 67 CE is doubted, but era agreed.
